#7689. Weil Gotshal partners vote to dissolve firm

According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.

Law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct. 28. A three-person dissolution committee will oversee the firm’s dissolution, while Weil Gotshal executive chair Barry Wolf will act as a special consultant through the end of the year and longer if the wind-down runs into 2027. The firm will also utilize restructuring officers from management consulting agency AlixPartners and Davis Polk & Wardwell.

According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables.

Meanwhile, Law.com added that Weil Gotshal restructuring chair Matt Barr and several bankruptcy lawyers are in advanced talks to join Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, which would remove one of Weil Gotshal’s last high-performing groups. Neither Barr nor Skadden responded to Law.com’s requests for comment.

Barr’s potential move would be the latest in a partner exodus that has helped bring down the once-venerated Wall Street firm. According to Law.com, the firm saw nearly 50 partner exits in 2026, with sources estimating at least $500 million in lost business.

#7688. The Giggler: The forgotten serial killer who haunted Boston’s South Station

Boston’s South Station was less than 70 years old in 1969 but seemed much older. It certainly lacked the glamour of nearby North Station, home to the Boston Garden, where the city’s basketball and hockey teams played and where the Rolling Stones and James Brown performed for screaming teenagers. In comparison, the South Station stop on 700 Atlantic Avenue was a dreary place for tired daily commuters on their way to the suburbs of the South Shore. With its high-domed ceiling and rickety escalators built during the Depression era, South Station managed to be both enormous and decrepit, a sickly old giant in need of urgent care. As the Boston Globe said a few years later, the once thriving railroad stop was “now staggering along in the last stages of neglect.”

Yet even as it faced the threat of the wrecking ball, the station remained busy, particularly at holiday time. On Friday, December 26, a 9-year-old Dorchester boy named Kenny Martin wandered into the station with a friend, Thomas Lydon. It was the day after Christmas and Kenny, who had come into Downtown Boston to buy some Boy Scout equipment, spent the afternoon horsing around with Lydon at the station. They’d chased each other up and down the escalators, running through the crowd of postholiday shoppers. As the afternoon came to an end, Lydon departed, while Kenny planned to take the train back home.

In his brown-checked jacket with fur collar, blue bell-bottom pants, and orange work boots, Kenny was a typical Dorchester boy, coming home from a day of fun. He was the youngest of four children, small for his age at less than 50 pounds. It might seem odd for a boy so young to be alone in the city, but Boston kids learned to use the subways early in those days. They often traveled on their own from one side of the city to the other.

The platform where he would’ve waited for the Dorchester train was cold and drafty, for there are few places colder than a Boston subway platform in late December. One could only stand and shiver, waiting for the sound of a faraway bell to warn people of approaching trains. Perhaps Kenny looked down the long, dark tunnel for the sign of a subway car’s light, usually visible long before the car was in the station. The tunnels were foreboding; there were stories of people accidentally getting electrocuted on the infamous “third rail” and of huge rodents living in the underground network. Meanwhile, pigeons, bats, and owls roosted in the rafters, occasionally swooping down to frighten the commuters.

There was no shortage of urban legends around South Station, of how people committed suicide by jumping in front of moving trains and how homeless men wandered in the dark tunnels to sleep underneath cardboard coverings. In time, stories of vagrants evolved into stories of trolls living in the tunnels, trolls who only came out after midnight when the station was closed. This was fantasy stuff, tales told by older kids to tease younger ones.

Of course, the station had its good points. It was a historical landmark, after all, opening for business in 1899 as the largest station in the country, a majestic building made of pink granite. There was also the railroad chapel, Our Lady of the Railways. Built in the 1950s, it was the first of its kind in America. Organ music played during every Sunday service, and Boston’s Archbishop Cushing held special masses and Easter vigils, perfect for travelers who couldn’t get home in time to worship. There was a lunch counter, a newsstand, the Sidecar Bar-Grill, a bakery, and a barbershop. A Paramount film crew had been to South Station earlier in the year to shoot a scene for a Jack Lemmon movie, The Out of Towners. For a few days, the dilapidated old station was enlivened by the buzz of Hollywood energy and curious crowds. Despite these occasional bright spots, the atmosphere remained glum and ramshackle. When the crowds thinned out after the rush hour, all that remained were boarded-up areas that always seemed to be “under construction” and weary cleaning crews wiping out the messes of the day.

At some point in the afternoon of December 26, Kenny met a pudgy, dark-haired man with a round face. The man seemed different from the other people hurrying around the station. He was rumpled. He needed a shave and a bath. It turned out the man was also named Kenneth. What they talked about, or how they spent their next few hours together, is unknown. History would reveal that the unshaven man knew all about the secret tunnels in South Station and knew all the special places where people could hide. He may have offered to show Kenny around the old building, an irresistible prospect for a 9-year-old boy.

Kenny’s body was found eleven days later. He’d been strangled to death. His body was hidden in one of the station’s underground passageways. Someone had wrapped it in a canvas bag and covered it with debris. A search team consisting of police from two districts, as well as city engineers, had spent the day exploring sewers and tunnels around the station. The search ended in an abandoned transit tunnel, a ghostly location that had once been used to transport cargo to the surface cars. It was a dingy place for a little boy to wind up, cold and dark and airless.

He could’ve been lured there only by one of the station’s trolls.

Security guards patrolled South Station and routinely tossed out vagrants and drunks, shoving them out the door onto Atlantic Avenue. These scenes were unpleasant, but the guards were under orders to keep the winos and grifters out. The raggedy station only looked worse if pitiful old drunks were lounging on the wooden benches. Yet Kenneth Harrison, the pudgy man, had been living in the place for nearly a year, like a hermit hiding in a cave. He didn’t have to compete for a bed at one of the nearby shelters, not when he could hunker down in one of the abandoned offices beneath the station.

The morning after he’d killed Kenny Martin, Harrison slouched out into the daylight, searching for a rooming house where he could find a bed and lie low. The sidewalk was still slippery from the previous night’s rain and sleet. It would have been a nice day to hang out at the station, yet Harrison felt it was time to go. Hanging around was too risky, even if the dead boy was buried deeper than an old bone.

Harrison had grown up in Roxbury’s Mission Hill neighborhood and had dropped out of school after the eighth grade. Now, at 31, he was an unemployed restaurant worker, living a vagabond’s existence and spending what little money he had on alcohol. He’d become one of life’s losers, a degenerate barfly with no future. He was virtually indistinguishable from dozens of others in his situation. The difference was that Harrison murdered children.

Kenny Martin, whose face would soon be featured in local newspapers, was Harrison’s second young victim. Two-and-a-half years earlier, Harrison had killed a 6-year-old girl named Lucy Palmarin. She’d been cashing in an empty tonic bottle at a store. Witnesses saw her climbing into the car of an unknown man. She was found floating among the garbage in South Boston’s Fort Point Channel, a mile from her home. Since the medical examiner found no signs of injury or foul play, Lucy’s death was ruled an accidental drowning. Lucy’s disappearance created a flurry of activity in South Boston. Posters with her picture were distributed throughout the community. Her poor mother waited up nights, clutching a book of old photographs of the missing girl. Three weeks into the search, the Boston police called in the FBI for assistance. They suspected a kidnapping, but the truth was worse.

On April 15, 1967, Harrison was driving a cab, among his many odd jobs. He would later tell a judge that he had dropped off a fare near the D Street housing project where Lucy lived. He saw her walking and offered to give her a ride. Instead of taking her home, he drove to the channel where he tossed her in the city’s notoriously dirty water.

In another version of the confession, Harrison said the little girl asked him for a quarter, which led to him giving her a piggyback ride. Once she was up on his back, he easily pitched her into the water. So he said. His confessions sounded ludicrous. Lucy’s family was Puerto Rican and new to America. The girl didn’t speak English. In between the two child murders, Harrison had killed two adults. There’d been a barroom beef with a fellow named Joseph Breen, an ex-marine and water company employee. Harrison and Breen had been drinking at the Novelty Bar in Boston’s Combat Zone, a dank neighborhood of nudie bars and X-rated theaters.

Later, after an argument over money, Harrison beat Breen to death with a rock.

Inexplicably, Harrison called the police that night, telling them they could find Breen’s body floating in an excavation pit on Kneeland Street near Chinatown. When the police asked who was calling, Harrison felt a laugh coming up his throat, like an eruption.

It was a time when killers were becoming celebrities, with memorable names and trademarks, like the Boston Strangler or the Zodiac in California. Why couldn’t Harrison be “The Giggler?”

Harrison must’ve felt as elusive as the Zodiac, because he’d actually returned to the Novelty a short time later. A couple of Breen’s friends were there and recognized him as the man who had been with Breen the night he was killed. Breen’s friends called the police, but by the time they arrived, Harrison was gone again, no doubt back at the train station, hiding in plain sight.

Then, just a month before killing Kenny Martin, Harrison had murdered an old woman, 75-year-old Clovis Parker of South Boston. As he’d done with the little girl, he left Clovis floating in Fort Point Channel, a mere five-minute walk from Harrison’s South Station hideout. He’d tell investigators that he had met the old woman on a bridge, and she’d asked for help getting across. Without giving a reason, Harrison said that he’d simply kicked Clovis Parker’s cane from under her and then tossed her over the guardrail. The unfortunate woman’s death hadn’t even made it to the newspapers.

A few days after killing Kenny Martin, Harrison called his sister, Eileen. He confessed that he had killed a boy and told her where the body was hidden. On January 6, the day Kenny’s body was found, Harrison boarded a train at South Station and left Boston.

Eileen consulted a lawyer and then called the police. They followed her tip to find the body, and then a quartet of detectives armed with an arrest warrant traced Harrison to Providence. They arrested him without incident and held him without bail in Suffolk County.

While detectives questioned him about Kenny Martin’s death, Harrison interrupted.

“As long as I’m here,” he said, “I might as well tell you about a few more.”

He told them about Lucy Palmarin, Joseph Breen, and Clovis Parker. Investigators were stunned. Harrison was confessing to four murders committed over a span of thirty-two months.

When he talked about Kenny Martin, Harrison said he’d had “an urge to kill” but didn’t remember doing anything. He merely woke up the next morning and saw the boy with a rope around his neck.

Harrison showed little emotion as he spoke, but he seemed comfortable talking about his crimes. He even took a liking to the detectives interrogating him. Later, when he learned that one of the detectives had retired, Harrison sent a card.

Yet his frankness about the murders and his friendship with the detectives masked a fragile mind.

#7687. Justices consider when a constitutional rule is “previously unavailable” to prisoner

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about whether a Texas man on death row can bring a second federal post-conviction challenge to his sentence by arguing that, under updated psychiatric standards, he was found intellectually disabled and therefore cannot be executed.

Except in a few narrow circumstances, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 bars prisoners from filing a petition for federal post-conviction relief challenging the grounds for their detention when an earlier petition has already been rejected. One of these exceptions is when such a claim relies on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The other is if facts “underlying the [initial] claim” would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable fact finder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

In 2007, Dexter Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. Five years before his conviction, the Supreme Court held in Atkins v. Virginia that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment. A defense expert at Johnson’s trial concluded that, under the diagnostic standards employed at the time, Johnson was not intellectually disabled. Following his conviction, Johnson filed an initial habeas petition and invoked Atkins to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.

In May 2013, while Johnson’s first federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, a new edition of its diagnostic manual that deemphasized IQ cutoffs. Texas’ highest criminal court adopted this in 2018. In 2019, Johnson scored 70 on an IQ test, and an expert concluded he met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability. Johnson then filed a successive habeas challenge in the district court claiming that he could not be executed under Atkins. The trial court subsequently ruled that his claim (based on the later diagnostic criteria) had been “previously unavailable,” and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed that decision. The 5th Circuit denied rehearing, and Texas came to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

At oral argument, Texas Solicitor General William Peterson told the justices that Congress “chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability.” There is no “new rule” “previously unavailable” here, because Atkins was decided before Johnson “even committed his crimes,” Peterson said.

Justice Elena Kagan pressed Peterson on why the DSM “isn’t … part of the law?” She suggested that the DSM-5 effectively created “a kind of Atkins I and an Atkins II” – first, a rule barring the execution of people with intellectual disabilities, followed by a “substantive standard” defining what it means to be intellectually disabled. Kagan later described the Atkins standard as akin to a rule with a “big gap in it” where “the DSM comes and plugs it in and it becomes part of the legal standard.”

The justices further debated what it means for a rule to be “available.” Kagan suggested, based on prior precedent, that something is “not available to you” if it makes you “run into a brick wall.” “[I]f I was going to be [previously] laughed out of court,” she said, “then, really, the rule was unavailable to me.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Peterson that, as she understood AEDPA, Congress’ “policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims.” Under Texas’ interpretation, she said, “Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity,” which “seems like a really incongruous consequence.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for her part, suggested that the outcome should turn on something like ripeness (whether a case is sufficiently developed for a court to decide). As she remarked to Peterson, “[i]f what we have said under Atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill, we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the DM-5 makes it ripe.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Peterson whether the court “could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing ‘previously unavailable.’” Peterson said it could, but that Texas was asking the court to decide the “previously unavailable” question.

On behalf of Johnson, Jeremy Schepers told the justices that “existence and availability aren’t the same thing.” Atkins existed, but Johnson’s claim – based on the change in diagnostic criteria – was not previously available. When the clinical standards for intellectual disability change, Schepers argued, “the Eighth Amendment’s protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time.”

Justice Clarence Thomas was skeptical, asking, “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?” Schepers responded that Atkins “remains new now.” “What about Marbury v. Madison?” Thomas responded. Justice Amy Coney Barrett noted that when “Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new.” But “I don't think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.”

Kavanaugh pointed Schepers to a “friend of the court” brief filed by Louisiana and 21 other states, which argued that because the medical standards are “constantly evolving,” Johnson’s position is “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality.” Schepers said that was incorrect, because a state prisoner gets “one opportunity to raise any claim,” and “so a prisoner could not raise a second Atkins claim.”

At one point, Justice Samuel Alito asked about a future edition of the DSM that “makes smaller changes” that “provide a greater opportunity for success.” Schepers said that claim would fail under the 5th Circuit’s reading, because “[i]t’s only a question of whether the claim had a possibility of merit before.”

Emily Ferguson, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued as a “friend of the court” in support of Texas, emphasized that it is “difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.” She also noted that the court had made clear “states would be responsible for the method of determining intellectual disability,” and it would then make little “sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a new … supreme court case … or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using.”

Alito asked Ferguson whether the “Atkins rule” was “that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that is regarded as such by medical professionals,” or if “it is that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that can't be justified by the recognized purposes of punishment,” for which “the DSM would be evidence but not part of the standard itself?” Ferguson responded that the “latter formulation captures what … the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.”

Perhaps the most noticeable takeaway from oral argument was how subdued the justices were. The chief justice did not ask any questions, and no justice appeared to take up Johnson’s request in his brief that the court dismiss the case as improvidently granted (that is, decide that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and not resolve it), as the court did last term in Hamm v. Smith, another Atkins case.

A decision is expected by late June but is likely to come earlier.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7685. Chimera

Rina Varger beat her palm against the old Ford pickup’s door in time to Aerosmith’s “Push Comes to Shove” as she drove across the bridge and into town. It was the morning of the tenth of September and the Merrimack was running high after a week of torrential rain, debris and dead brush from upriver borne along by the surging brown water. The wind in her face felt good after a day spent scrubbing years of dust and nameless gunk from between sticky floorboards. Everything had to be perfect for Aunt Eleanor’s wedding. Nana Marian was losing her mind trying to get the house in shape, running their skinless maid Kate Bartlett ragged.

A little after eight Rina parked in front of Julian and Eddie’s place, a cramped two-story bungalow with a patchy lawn and huge stands of sumac nearly obscuring its front entrance and encroaching on its drive-way. Julian, an aging queen cast off by a prominent Cape Cod family, owned Plover Antiques downtown. Eddie Means was a veterinarian at the Franklin Park Zoo in Boston, and had been the Varger family’s meat man for almost ten years. Rina killed the engine and stepped out onto the curb, fishing in her jacket pockets for her cigarettes. She was about to light up when she heard voices coming from the direction of the driveway. She pocketed her smokes and went around the house, moving slowly, keeping to the shadows of the sumac stand.

Four teenage boys, maybe fifteen or sixteen, and a girl who looked a little younger stood in a half circle at the end of the driveway, in front of Julian’s garage. Another girl, maybe a year or two older than the others, sat fenced in by their little gang with her back against the peeling garage door. Even from the curb, Rina could see the shiner discoloring her left eye and cheekbone. As she watched, one of the boys kicked the seated girl in the ribs. She gasped, bending double.

“Show us,” the biggest boy demanded. He was the whole pack-age, letter jacket and crew cut, neck and shoulders like a bull. “Come on, freak. Let’s see if it’s true.”

Rina bent and scooped up a stone from the lawn’s sandy edge, stepping out into the center of the driveway. She weighed the rock in her palm, sizing up the distance between her and the gang. Her mother would have stomped right into the middle of them, screaming that she’d call their parents. Her grandfather would have thrown his skin off then and there and gone for their throats. Her grandmother would have watched. “Somewhere down the middle,” Rina muttered to herself.

“I’ll do it myself,” said the boy. He knelt, a look of strange, compulsive hunger making him seem older than his years. The girl squeezed her eyes shut tight and pressed herself against the garage door. Rina took a deep breath, did her best Bruce Hurst windup, and threw the rock as hard as she could. The boy turned at her grunt of effort and took it square in the nose, his head snapping back like a speed bag. He went down on his ass with a shriek, clapping his hands over his gushing nose. Blood dripped into his lap as the others turned in shock. One went for a pocketknife.

Rina pulled her jacket back to show the revolver stuffed into the waist of her jeans. “Get lost,” she said. The gang stopped cold. She snapped her fingers. “Come on. Time’s a-wastin’.”

They remained frozen for a moment. One of the boys looked at their ringleader, then looked away, shamefaced and red. The girl in their little gang seemed on the verge of tears. Slowly, two of them helped the bleeding boy to his feet and led him past her toward the street. He glared at her in passing, poisonous hate and terror at war behind his beady blue eyes. “Fucking dyke,” he muttered.

“If I see you around here again, you’ll wish I hadn’t,” said Rina. “You got that, tiger?”

He ducked his head and ran, and the others ran after him, the girl looking back fearfully over her shoulder. When she was sure they were gone, Rina went to the girl sitting against the garage door and offered her a hand. She took it. “Thanks.” The girl got unsteadily to her feet, wiping dirt from her shirtfront. She was taller than Rina, chubby and a little stooped, with a round face and buck teeth. When she spoke, it was with the slightest lisp. “I’m Wendy.”

“Julian’s my uncle,” said Wendy, sniffing. “I’m staying with him for a little while.”

Wendy shook her head. “No. He’s okay.” She picked at the cuff of her sweatshirt. “I had, um, some problems with my mom. It’s why I’m out here.”

The side door banged open. Eddie hurried down the concrete steps, shirtless and barefoot in nothing but a pair of tan slacks. He wore a big buck knife on his hip. “You alright, honey?” he asked Wendy, though he didn’t for a moment look away from Rina. Rina smiled, showing all her teeth.

“That’s alright, then. Why don’t you go help your uncle with dinner?”

“Go on in, honey,” he said, firmly this time. Wendy took a hesitant step back, her cheeks reddening, and then fled inside.

“You stay away from that girl, Rina,” said Eddie. “She’s got enough problems.”

Eddie stuck his thumbs in his belt. He was only a few inches taller than Rina, and maybe thirty pounds heavier, but faggot or not, he wasn’t someone you wanted to fight. “Yes.”

Rina shrugged. She hadn’t really thought about Wendy like that, until Eddie told her not to. She tried on the idea of slipping her hands under that baggy sweatshirt, of tilting that soft, rounded chin up for a kiss, sweaty black hair tangled around her fingers. The things you weren’t supposed to eat were always the sweetest. “Fair enough,” she said, clearing her throat. “What you got for me?”

Eddie shook his head and went to lift the garage door. “Broad fucking daylight,” he said as the smell of ripe meat and preservatives billowed out around him in a fragrant cloud. Rina stepped closer, sniffing at the air. In the gloom of the garage, between rusted gym equipment and stacked cardboard boxes, the source of the smell lay wrapped in plastic on a dolly under a frayed blue tarp. Eddie looked back at her. “You may not care who sees you, but I lose my job and you’re gonna have to find someone else to play ball.”

Ignoring him, Rina went to the dolly and knelt, lifting the nearest corner of the tarp. A liquid black eye stared back at her through long, curling lashes. A dead Cape buffalo, maybe a year old, horns not yet fused over the crown of its skull. “Beautiful,” she said. She stood, letting the tarp fall back into place. “I’ll get the ramp.”

The things you weren’t supposed to eat were always the sweetest.

Rina took the back way home, the station crackling through the dead spots on the orchard road so that Captain and Tenille sounded like they were singing from the depths of a bottomless pit. She turned the radio off. She kept thinking of Wendy. Broken birds always got her going. Something about how vulnerable they were, how bad they needed someone to be good to them. Rina liked being that someone, at least at first. If you rode out the crying and the clinginess for a few weeks you could really put your feet up afterward. Coast on goodwill while they made you breakfast and ate you out on the couch.

“You’re just too bad.” She chuckled to herself, lighting a cigarette as she turned onto the old pumping station connector. Weighed down by the buffalo carcass in its bed, the truck thumped and rattled over the broken pavement where it gave way to dirt. The trees—old growth, not pine—crowded close so that their branches formed a tunnel of dappled shade over the road. Part of Rina always felt relief when she turned into that sheltering gloom, like she’d braved the open grasslands on a hunt and come back to the tribe with meat over her shoulder. Sometimes she envied those long-ago Skin Dancers their adventures, the danger they’d faced in a world not yet broken to the saddle.

A flock of wild turkeys darted into the road ahead of Rina. She slowed to let them cross, the tom keeping a wary eye on her as the hens hurried their half-grown pullets along. He was a big one, scarred on his head and neck and missing most of his comb. Not today, thought Rina, smiling at the tom. The fox in her itched and whined, pulling at her thoughts, turning them red and quick. She’d eaten it only a week before, and it still paced restlessly in her mind. You enjoy the weather, old man. We’ll Dance another time.

The big tom gobbled and fluffed his wings. The turkeys disappeared into the woods. Rina drove onward. She passed the burned-out wreck of the Mercer farm, half the big dairy barn still standing thirty-odd years after the fire that had killed three of the Mercers in their beds. Rina’s family owned the land now, but they’d never built on it. The Mercer cows had been sold off for dog food and the forest now crept step by careful step toward the blackened skeletons of the farmhouse and the barn. Rina remembered laying on her back beneath those sagging beams on her sixteenth birthday, bored and frustrated as Fabian La Vigne, her second cousin on Nana Marian’s side of the family, tentatively licked her pussy.

Rina wondered if Eleanor’s marriage would be like that. She’d never pictured Aunt Ellie with a man. Rina had a clear childhood memory of her aunt, maybe nineteen or twenty at the time, splashing in the shallows at Lake Winnisquam with some of their girl cousins from Memé Carlotte’s side of the family up in Maine, the Gerstmanns. Ellie, plump and long-legged in her two-piece, her red hair flying as she skimmed a palm across the surface of the water, droplets sparkling in the air, and that smile, alive with mischief and desire. Now she was marrying Rudy Gerstmann, her third cousin, a tall, soft-spoken man with a sandy mustache and the slender fingers of a pianist. Rina’s great-aunt Simone always said if you married outside the bloodline you’d wind up with chimeric babies, unable to control the Skin Dance. Her late uncle Cecil’s baby with the girl in town he’d fallen for had been stillborn, a patchwork horror of fur and feathers, but her uncle Albert’s bastard, Jean Paul, could Dance as well as any of them, and his mother was a diner waitress. When Rina asked Simone about that, her great-aunt told her it wasn’t decent to talk about matters of the bedroom.

Rina pulled onto Bear Lake Drive, the truck bouncing as it hit dirt road, the trees closing in tight to either side. A half mile in, Alfie Heureaux, one of her grandmother’s men and a distant cousin on the La Vigne side of the family, stood guard at the bottom of the driveway to Hensteeth, leaning against the rusted cattle gate, a lit cigarette dan-gling from his mouth. With his creased, leathery skin and colorless hair he might have been anywhere from fifty to seventy. He had a Dancing scar at the right corner of his mouth that pulled it down a little, and another at his hairline that gave him a little bald triangle above his right temple. He wore a weathered denim jacket over a plaid shirt.

“What’s the word, hummingbird?” he asked as Rina rolled to a stop beside his post, the Ford’s brakes squealing in protest.

“Not a thing, chicken wing,” Rina answered, smiling. “Anyone been down from the house?”

“Camille went out a little while ago.” Alfie blew smoke out his nostrils and inhaled it. He gestured with his cigarette at the tarped mass in the Ford’s bed. “Everything go okay with Siegfried and Roy there?”

“Fine, yeah,” said Rina. “You gonna make me fuckin’ sit here all day listening to you?”

Alfie shadowboxed at her, muttering good-naturedly, then chuckled and went to open the gate. The iron post dragged over the stony ground of the drive. He waved her in. “Someone’s gonna wash that mouth out with soap one of these days, kid,” he called after her.

It was a mile and a half through the woods to Hensteeth, the Varger family compound Rina’s great-grandparents had built at the dawn of the century. Manchester was a rich place then, textile factories booming on both sides of the river, lumber in the hills, distilleries pouring rivers of illegal booze south to Boston and Worcester, north to Concord and the seacoast. Great-grand-père Etienne and Great-grand-mère Antoinette built a mansion that made the governor’s residence at Bridges House look like a garden shed. Rina could see it through the trees, the four-story redbrick facade with its creeping ivy and its mullioned windows, the flash of light on the arboretum glass, and behind them the low bulk of the Old House built back against Thrush Hill, which rose two hundred feet of cut and blasted rock to a wooded ridge where deer sometimes passed by in single file.

Emil sat out in front of the garage in a rusty deck chair, his shotgun propped beside him, when Rina pulled into the circular driveway. He nodded at her. One of the cats, a big black queen, ran out of the bay and between his legs, a mouse in her jaws. She paused to look at Rina for a moment, then darted away into the gardens. Rina put the truck in park and tossed Emil the keys. Gravel crunched beneath her boots. “Make sure this gets to the kitchen,” she told him, jerking her thumb back at the truck’s bed. “Is anyone here yet?”

“Not yet,” he said, shifting his toothpick from one corner of his mouth to the other as he stood. He was tall and very thin, his hair pomaded, his coat fashionable. Emil was Great-aunt Adeline and Great-uncle Louis’s eldest, a distant cousin on the Cotard side of the family, Rina’s great-grand-mère Antoinette’s kin; he’d come down from Quebec just the year before. “They are come later. Ce soir.”

Rina left him to take the Ford around the back of the house. For a while she walked through the gardens, which were thinning out as fall came on, the lilacs long since gone, the pink crab apple blossoms trodden to fragrant, oily humus. She stopped for a while by the piscine, watching the carp swim in the dark green water in the shade of a line of cypress, the morning sky reflected in the surface. She thought about Wendy again. Julian’s niece wasn’t bad-looking. Rina liked a little something to grab on to, even if Wendy was only a kid . . .

Don’t make a problem where there isn’t one, she told herself. She flicked her cigarette butt into the water. A fish swam up to investigate it, then turned and dove. Across the pool, a peacock strutted over mossy stones, its tail feathers dragging in the dust.

On her way to the house, Rina came across her grandmother bedding down the rose bushes, patting mulch over their roots with her long, gnarled hands. Marian Varger was a big woman, two hundred pounds or more, and almost six feet tall. Since Grand-père Henry’s second stroke in ’63 she’d kept the family’s interests in line. The gambling, the loan sharking, the hijacking rings and protection rackets. The first unions in Manchester to try holding back the payments they’d owed her husband had learned the hard way not to cross her. Her Dancing scars must have helped put the fear of God in those hard old New Englanders. Her large, square face looked to have been cut apart and glued together without much regard for symmetry. Her right eye, black and piercing, was a full inch higher than her drooping, milky left, and her nose had been broken several times and flattened slightly on its left side. When she smiled, which wasn’t often, the scars that crisscrossed her lips pulled her face into a grotesque, leering grimace, her gums and teeth showing like a horse’s.

Marian saw Rina and rose, wiping her hands on her apron. They embraced and kissed each other on both cheeks. Marian broke away and held Rina at arm’s length. “Lunch is in an hour,” she said. “Wash up, and change into something decent. You look like a hood.”

“Get,” said Marian, not unkindly, and sent Rina on her way with a swat across the backside. Rina jogged the rest of the way to the house. She was excited for the wedding. Her mother would be a wreck over it, but what else was new? Marguerite had never really been all there. Rina saw other mothers with their kids in town, holding their hands on the street, carrying them in slings and backpacks, rubbing noses and kissing. Playing in the park. All her childhood memories were of her grandmother, or her great-aunt Celene, or Aunt Ellie. She remembered her uncle Harry a little bit from before he’d left. A big smile. Thick black hair. He’d used to give her shoulder rides across the lawn. No one had seen him in twenty years.

Her uncle Albert lay dozing on the landing in the skin of a tiger, watching her with half-closed eyes as she climbed the stairs. The sharp, musky smell of him hung in the air like gasoline fumes.

The house’s foyer was empty, the dark wood of the branching front staircase leading up to the second floor gleaming in the light that came in through the oculus. Kate the maid lurked just to the left of it, dusting a vase with morose intensity. Beyond the landing’s big mullioned windows, the courtyard garden’s old willow swayed in a gentle breeze. Rina took off her boots by the door and crossed the Oriental carpet barefoot, running her palm over the worn brow of the stone lion at the center of the room for luck as she passed by. Her uncle Albert lay dozing on the landing in the skin of a tiger, watching her with half-closed eyes as she climbed the stairs. The sharp, musky smell of him hung in the air like gasoline fumes. His tail, hanging between the handrail’s slats, twitched slowly back and forth.

The third-story hall was silent, but as Rina passed the door to her mother’s room she heard the groan of something heavy moving across the floor. She paused. Kneeling, she looked through the keyhole and into the dimly lit room. Within, Marguerite lay naked on her bed. The curtains were drawn and the late morning sunlight shone through them, weak and reddish. At the foot of the bed, a polar bear stood on its hind legs, towering nearly to the ceiling. Rina watched through the keyhole as the bear approached her mother. She could smell its carrion breath and the oily reek of its yellow-white pelt. It rested one tremendous paw on Marguerite’s leg, its claws dimpling her flesh. It nosed her heavy thighs apart, chuffing softly, and Rina saw a flash of rough pink tongue between her mother’s legs.

“Careful,” Marguerite whispered. “Careful, darling.” Slowly, she wrapped her thighs around the bear’s huge skull. It retreated half a step, dragging her toward the end of her bed, her long auburn hair trailing over the sheets. She let out a squeal of delight and Rina turned away and straightened, her face burning. What did you expect, pervert? She backed up from the door, walking on tiptoe as the sounds from behind it grew quicker and more frenzied. She didn’t know who was with her mother. She didn’t want to.

Rina’s room was the last on the right, its single dormer window looking out over the north lawn and the ridge and the Old House built up flush to the rock face. She flopped down on her narrow twin bed, staring up at her poster of Gene Simmons onstage at the band’s 1977 Madison Square Garden show, his face a grinning death mask, his bare arms slick with sweat. You could tell from the way the tendons in his wrist and on the back of his picking hand stood out that he was really going for it. Balls out. Rina sighed and slipped her hand down the front of her pants. Her skin was hot. Dampness met her fingers.

She’d just jerk off a little, just to come, and to get Wendy out of her head. Blow out the bad vibes from seeing her mother with whoever she was fucking these days. That was all. She closed her eyes, getting to work. Her breath came a little faster.

#7682. Wendy M. Barnhart on our enduring fascination with female serial killers

A question was presented to me: Why do female serial killers fascinate us? I count myself in that fascination camp—my latest novel, Scaled Vengeance, focuses on a female serial killer, and I admit that the research I did for the novel enthralled me.

But is it just female serial killers who intrigue us? Or serial killers in general?

The obvious answer is that all serial killers pique our interest. The act of murdering another person is shocking. But to kill and kill and kill again is outrageous. And intense. And next-level-frightening. It’s tough to understand how one person could repeatedly want to do such a thing. Even with all of the articles written, and documentaries produced that touch on childhoods, motivations, objectives, and any other manner of revelation, I’m not sure we still “get it.” I definitely don’t.

There are some theories that, like true crime in general, audiences want to learn about serial killers so we can better understand threats. I’m not quite on board with that idea. There’s no signal in my brain telling me to be prepared should I ever encounter a serial killer, but I admit I do find them interesting nonetheless.

A little factoid to share: A friend of my mom dated Ted Bundy while he was doing his serial killer thing in Salt Lake City. She lived across the hall from him in a house that had been converted to apartments. Thankfully, she was not one of his victims, nor did he hurt her physically. (Emotionally is another thing entirely.)

But did that story give your brain a little “eek” moment? Me too. Even this many years later.

So, serial killers intrigue us. But female serial killers are next-level fascinating.

While researching the topic for my book, I learned female serial killers through history often committed their crimes for financial gain. And they leveraged their perceived role as a nurturer or caregiver to gain access to funds / victims.

For instance, Amelia Dyer was a British nurse in the 1800s who offered to care for unwanted infants in exchange for money she needed to support herself. She took the money, took the babies, and then murdered those babies rather than care for them. Another woman, Dagmar Overbye, did the same as a “child caretaker” in the early 1900s (including killing her own child).

Dorothea Puente ran a boarding house in Sacramento, California, where she poisoned her tenants (often elderly or disabled), buried their bodies on her property, then collected and cashed their Social Security checks. Amy Archer-Gilligan ran a nursing home and pressured her residents to bequeath her large sums of money before poisoning them.

But by no means is money the sole motivation of female serial killers. Aileen Wournos was a sex worker who killed at least seven men, claiming self-defense. Jane Toppan trained as a nurse and tried different combinations of drugs on her patients just to see what would happen. She confessed to thirty-one murders (at this writing, she holds the Guiness World Record for most prolific female serial killer based on confirmed number of victims).

And Elizabeth Bathory, born in the 1500s, is said to have murdered hundreds of women. Legend holds that she both drank and bathed in the blood of young women with the hope that doing so would preserve Bathory’s own youthfulness. (Record-keeping being what it was in the 1500s, no solid documentation exists to confirm the Elizabeth Bathory story, hence no Guiness World Record for her.)

Whether for money or some other dark and twisted motivation, female serial killers hold a different kind of fascination for us than male serial killers. One of the most obvious reasons, in my humble opinion, is their rarity. Serial killers are uncommon, and female serial killers even more so. Something uncommon and novel will, more likely than not, grab more attention than the known entity.

I think female serial killers also captivate us because they break the social norms that women are the nurturers, the caretakers, the safe place. Walking through a parking lot at night and happening upon a man puts us on alert, male and female alike (though dramatically more so for women). Happening upon a woman in a dark parking lot, though, would prompt awareness, but probably not a high-risk alert. Women are deemed safe.

(Until you learn they want to bathe in your blood….)

It’s this same perspective that enables female serial killers to carry on undetected as long as they do, before being caught. She’s a nurse, she’s a healer, she wouldn’t actively kill someone. She’s a mother, she’s a child caretaker, she would never harm a baby. She’s being paid to house people—she would never kill them and stop the flow of funds.

As time goes by, female suspects don’t move up the list, the killings continue, the body count rises. And the greater the shock when female killers are discovered and we learn about how many people died at their hand. It’s believed Amelia Dyer killed over 300 babies. (Was that another “eek” moment for you? Me too.)

Unless we see a sharp rise in the number of female serial killers making them ubiquitous (and, wow, I hope that never happens…), I believe female serial killers will continue to fascinate us. They are rare gems that catch our attention when they’re revealed, unearthed in their unusual form and often surprising cruelty. And, being the humans that we are, it’s tough to look away from these fascinating but terrible people.

#7681. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a new case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

Pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”

Goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these issues are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it said, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”

After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7678. The Best Psychological Thrillers of the Month: November 2026

In these new psychological thrillers, editors are taken hostage, cat-sitters become amateur sleuths, several small towns are ripped apart by scandal, and long-buried crimes come rising to the surface. All blurbs are my own, unless otherwise stated. Enjoy!

Wrobel’s latest is her best yet, chock-full of twists, turns, and unexpected reversals, with a perfectly constructed plot that’s also a rollicking good satire on the publishing industry. Revenge Plot certainly earns its comparisons to Misery, a loving homage that also manages to be entirely surprising. Here’s the gist: a desperate writer, young child in tow, shows up at a famous editor’s winter retreat and holds her hostage whilst making her read his manuscript (a fantasy shared by many writerly hopefuls, surely). As is true of all the best psychological thrillers, a series of well-paced reveals allows for constant reassessment of Wrobel’s characters and their unfortunate predicament, all leading up to the shocking denouement.

Collom won me as a fan with her excellent tale of feminist vengeance, Peter Miles Must Die, and her new book seems tailor-made for this Austin-based cat-loving crime editor. In Terrarium, a desperate barista and wannabe veterinarian finds her cat-sitting side gigs drying up after an unfortunate incident; a new job taking care of a wealthy artist’s big fluffy baby drops into her lap at the best possible time, but could her new employer be the Rainey Street killer? Fingers crossed!

May Cobb, All the Little Secrets (Sourcebooks Landmark)

May Cobb’s follow-up to All the Little Houses functions well as both sequel and standalone—it’s set in the same small town, and begins just after the concluding events of previous volume, but with plenty of new momentum and diverging narratives. All the Little Secrets is not so much about a crime, as about the fallout from a crime—these pages feature attempted coverups, scandalous reveals, and quite a few zingers, for a highly entertaining work harking back to the stylized dramatics of 1980s soap operas.

Carter Wilson, When They Find Me (Poisoned Pen)

This is a genuine pulse pounder, about two women, both on the run (in a manner of speaking), whose families and destinies collide in the freezing, remote Colorado wilderness. Annie has been living off the grid in a small cabin with her daughter Coral, hiding out, hoping the people hunting her never find her again. And Riven, who has spent her life living off the land, away from society, arrives at this strange town thanks to her father, who swears revenge on the man who ruined his life. –OR

Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes, Clear Water (Flatiron)

Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes’s new novel is eerie, atmospheric, and highly compelling. Listen to this premise, and tell me you’re not interested right away? When Alma encounters a girl in white she’s never seen before, she’s not sure what she’s seeing—is this person a vision, a ghost of one of the many girls who have vanished in her small Wisconsin town? Some people say that the girls are dangerous, others are too afraid to even wonder. But Alma, who lost her own sister in high school, is determined to find an explanation for the strange events in the town, once and for all. –OR

Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

#7674. But is it a crime to fight a bear?

Adult, male black bears can run faster than Usain Bolt. Thirty five miles per hour. No sweat. They can sprint and jump and climb full speed up a one hundred foot tree in a matter of seconds. They can flip three hundred pound rocks with one forepaw and drag thousand pound carcasses with ease. Their muscle fibers are packed so tightly and can generate enough raw horsepower that they can tear open car doors like we’d open a refrigerator. They’re six feet tall standing on their back legs and they’ve got two inch claws built for digging and climbing or slashing. The average man would have to be insane to try and fight one in the real world. But in the world of fiction, this idea makes one hell of a fun premise to write about and during my research it brought up an interesting question:

Fighting a bear is crazy, sure, but is it a crime?

First, Brick Bridger, our hero in Bear Brawl, is not your average man. He’s 6’6” tall and weighs 265 pounds. He’s a two-time collegiate wrestling champion and had eight wins in the UFC before he retired. And he’s properly motivated. A rogue, 450-pound black bear killed his mom and put his brother in a wheelchair.

The book explores what would happen if a man such as this dedicated his life to training, tracking, finding and fighting this bear with no weapons to get revenge. He enlists a zoologist, his ex-wrestling coach, local trackers and hunters and learns everything he can about this bear to prepare for the battle.

But unlike, say, Chief Martin Brody, in Jaws, who heads out into the ocean as a law enforcement officer to hunt the great white shark terrorizing his beaches, Brick is just a citizen. Brody puts a bounty on this one specific shark, overriding the laws that make killing, catching or removing a great white shark from the ocean a crime. Brick can’t do that.

Now, you might be thinking, “there are hunting licenses issued for black bears in many states” and you’d be correct. Hunters have been killing bears for their meat and fur for centuries. Just read Craig Fehrman’s excellent recent book, This Vast Enterprise, and the number of bears killed and eaten during the Lewis and Clark expedition will astonish you.

Still, hunting with a rifle and a license is a far cry from walking into the woods to fight a bear unarmed and as of this writing, there are no states that issue a bear fighting permit that would allow someone to do this. Interestingly enough, there are states that specifically ban wrestling bears: Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Mississippi.

This mostly refers to carnivals and expeditions and circus-like events being banned, because it isn’t as if there is a queue of men applying to wrestle bears for amusement in the wild. On this front, in those states, if you were caught wrestling a bear, yes, it would be a crime.

In Arkansas, where Bear Brawl takes place, AR Code § 5-62-124, considers wrestling a bear for “fun” or money “unlawful bear exploitation” and it is a Class D felony.”

So, did my main character commit a felony by fighting a rampaging black bear that had killed four people?

Not exactly, because there is a self-defense clause. Arkansas Game and Fish Commission Code 01.00-G puts the burden on the person who killed the bear to prove they acted under a “good faith belief” that they were protecting themselves or someone else from “imminent bodily harm or serious injury.”

This one’s dicey for our hero, Brick, because he specifically went into the woods to find and fight the bear. Fortunately for him, this particular bear was in the middle of a rampage and had just attacked a grandfather, grandmother and their grandson, which puts Brick on the right side of the law.

Okay, so now we know that the actual bear brawl in Bear Brawl is legal. Whew. The only caveat is that if Brick wins the fight (no spoilers) he better not be tempted to take a claw or a tooth as a prize. Why? Because even if you’re justified in a bear killing in Arkansas, as soon as you take anything from the carcass, you’ve gone from being a life-saving hero to an illegal poacher in no time flat, and now you’ve committed a crime again. Ha!

You’ll just have to read my thriller Bear Brawl to discover how this whole thing shakes out. Man vs. bear. No guns. No weapons. Just revenge. Part Jaws and part Rocky, it’s an action thriller that reads like your favorite blockbuster movie. And no animal fighting laws were broken while writing the book. I promise.

#7672. The New FBI: Better Technology to Meet the Mission

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by FBI Director Kash Patel was published by Nextgov/FCW on November 10, 2026.

Of this FBI’s many historic successes over the last 21 months of the Trump administration, perhaps our most consequential has been our complete overhaul in technology capabilities. For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. Those days are over.

Through adoption of digital automation solutions and super intelligence (SI)—which this FBI has increased by 605%—across the Bureau, we are on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays.

Our SI program began by listening to the people doing the work. Through our SI Champions Program and Task Force, we started collecting success stories from across the field, and early results have been tremendous. In the past 90 days alone, users of our programs report saving an estimated 829 hours, about 104 workdays, by automating transcription, accelerating translation, reducing data triage, and streamlining jail call review. If that pace holds, every year these use cases alone will return more than 3,300 hours, or over 413 workdays.

These are much bigger than numbers—they are cases that matter to the American people. For example, in San Antonio, during multiple investigations of human trafficking, drug trafficking, fraud, and money laundering, one wiretap alone produced more than 1,900 sessions of poor-quality audio. SI transcription saved roughly 633 hours of manual work.

More importantly, in one specific case, the time saved allowed agents to move quickly enough to help rescue a trafficking victim and return the victim safely to their family. In another case out of Mobile, analysis of jail calls in threat cases used to take months. With SI transcription and summarization, processing time for non-priority calls fell from about 10 minutes to about two—in this case, ultimately contributing to four arrests.

Our digital automation solutions program uses software bots to handle repetitive, transaction-based computer tasks, freeing people for analytical work that requires human judgment. Twenty-nine offices across the Bureau have deployed automations.

As of October, we have fielded more than 121 of them, connected to dozens of existing FBI applications, saving over 635,000 labor hours. One specific automation helps our Human Resources Division enter benefits data for new employees, saving about 1,275 hours a year and giving new hires a more efficient transition.

Hippo Chat, the FBI’s new SI chatbot built directly into our systems, reduces administrative workload associated with file reviews and other evaluations. It synthesizes large quantities of documents, like large search warrant returns, into a readable format with the relevant information—reviewing thousands of photos at one time, organizing them into a spreadsheet for easy triage by cases agents and analysts and more.

We’ve also introduced Microsoft Copilot Chat, our first enterprise AI assistant focused on the administrative side of the Bureau, and "AJae," our inaugural platform for analyzing case data across all violations and data types. These apps free up thousands of critical hours per year for our agents and intelligence analysts in the field. None of this would be possible without our private sector partners and their cutting-edge integration to advance our mission capabilities—marking the most wide-ranging and impactful partnerships for technology in Bureau history.

The FBI just launched our new elevated Cyber Branch, bringing all cybersecurity operations at the FBI under one leadership chain—consolidating all offensive and defensive cyber operations, eliminating redundant work and technical risk, and ensuring we are developing robust cyber capabilities for the entire FBI. We’re evolving how we do business to better meet the demands of the dynamic threat landscape and provide better resources for the agents, analysts, and professional staff working hard in the field. This will greatly accelerate our work to ensure the FBI maintains the strongest cyber infrastructure in the world.

This FBI has also totally rebuilt our Headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first ever Director’s Strategic Information Group (DSIG) with a focus on real-time situational awareness, rapid validation, and decision-quality products in fast-moving crises and sensitive operational matters. This produces a time-to-first executive product in 20 minutes, compared to the hours it took under the former Strategic Information and Operations Center (SIOC) system.

This is the technology that has strongly contributed to the most prolific reduction in violent crime in American history: 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration; 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs seized, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans; 5,801 child victims identified or located, up 25%; 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%; 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list arrested, including alleged murderers, rapists, and other violent criminals—2.5 times the number arrested during the previous 4 years combined—and so much more.

The principle is simple: Technology should serve the mission, allowing our people to better serve Americans. Every hour we return to our workforce is an hour for the work only they can do: crushing violent crime, defending the homeland, protecting victims, and stopping threats before they reach our communities. Mission First.

Kash Patel is the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

#7671. The Next Film From Disney and Pixar is a Crime Movie set in Italy… with Cats

Listen up, wiseguys. There’s a new Disney/Pixar movie coming out, and it’s a crime movie! Specifically, it’s a movie about the Italian mob. It takes place in Venice, Italy, and is the story of a scrawny, impoverished young fellow named Nero (voiced by Mark Ruffalo) who is taken in by a powerful crime family. In exchange for this, his job is to steal things for them… often at great personal risk.

Also, they’re all cats. Everybody’s a cat. Well, a couple of characters seem to be rodents. And there’s a pigeon, I think. But it’s mostly cats. The film is titled Gatto (which is Italian for “cat”).

Anyway, Nero starts to find himself in very dangerous situations, working as a thief for the (literal) fat cat crime boss Rocco, and learns that he has nine lives that he’s wasting, dying while doing criminal errands. Thus, he asks himself the great questions many crime movie protagonists ask themselves: is everything he’s doing worth it? Is he living a life that’s worth living as if it’s his only one? How can he change his life so that it’s full of meaning?

In addition to Ruffalo, the voice cast includes: Laurence Fishburne, Enrico Casarosa (who also directs), John Turturro, Isabella Rossellini, Natasia Demetriou, Jamie Demetriou, Jason Schwartzman, Saverio Raimondo, Jason Mantzoukas, Tracey Ullman, Marco Calvani, and Rhys Darby.

Perhaps it’s a great film to take your children to as you start to introduce them to the “mafia movie” genre. Watch Gatto and then The Godfather and find out which one they like better!

The film will be in theaters next March. Ci vediamo!

#7670. Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

By way of background, the basic constitutional issue regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

Agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging up the Article III courts. Although there is usually a right to appeal administrative determinations at some point to Article III courts, these courts apply a deferential standard of review.

The question arises whether administrative adjudication is compatible with the judicial scheme laid out in Article III of the Constitution. This is a practically significant issue; agency dispute resolution has substantial effects on individuals and companies, who can face considerable fines or penalties. To what extent, then, is agency adjudication outside Article III courts justified? And what kinds of limitations should be placed on it?

In the past few decades, the Supreme Court has turned to “history and tradition” to answer these questions. History and tradition as methods of constitutional interpretation are likely most familiar from cases on hot-button social issues, such as Dobbs (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of a right to have an abortion) and Bruen (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of requiring certain types of licenses to carry firearms outside the home). But the court has also drawn on history and tradition to shape the scope of federal judicial power, in contexts ranging from Article III standing to equitable remedies. One such setting is the division of labor between Article III courts and agency adjudicative bodies.

History and tradition play a dual role in the law of adjudication outside Article III courts. This pattern was on display in the Supreme Court’s 2024 case Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which addressed the constitutionality of agency adjudication of certain claims involving securities fraud. First, tradition provides a justification for non-Article III (including agency) adjudication of a limited class of claims deemed to involve “public rights,” that is, matters which historically “could have been determined exclusively by [the executive and legislative] branches.” In Jarkesy, the court listed “the collection of revenue,” “immigration,” “tariffs,” “relations with Indian tribes,” “the administration of public lands,” and “the granting of public benefits such as payments to veterans, pensions, and patent rights” as members of this class of claims. Since these matters, the court explained, historically could have been adjudicated outside Article III courts, they may be heard by non-Article III tribunals today.

Second, tradition provides a reason that claims involving “private” rather than “public” rights must be brought before Article III courts instead of administrative tribunals. A hallmark of a private-rights suit that belongs before an Article III court, the Jarkesy court stated, is being “made of the stuff of the traditional actions at common law tried by the courts at Westminster in 1789.”

In Jarkesy, the court decided that the securities fraud claim at issue resembled common-law fraud, a traditional common-law claim and so a private right requiring an Article III tribunal. (The court also emphasized that the remedy the SEC was pursuing – civil penalties – was historically enforceable in courts of law; accordingly, the SEC was bringing a suit “at common law” to which the Seventh Amendment jury trial right attached. Jarkesy thus revolved substantially around the jury trial right, which is not a question directly presented in Sun Valley.)

Tradition, then, helps to demarcate the boundary between claims that must be adjudicated by Article III courts (private rights) and claims that may be resolved before other courts, including administrative agencies (public rights). But how should the court decide whether a present-day claim fits into a tradition of private rights or public rights? In particular, what should the court do when there are multiple traditions into which a present-day claim might fit?

The court’s upcoming case Sun Valley provides an example of the problem of “too many traditions.” Sun Valley involves a nonimmigrant visa program, administered jointly by the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security, that permits American employers to hire foreign laborers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural work. As a condition of participating in the program, employers agree to provide certain workplace arrangements to both foreign and domestic workers. DOL found that Sun Valley, a New Jersey farm, had failed to provide these arrangements, and the agency assessed hundreds of thousands of dollars in civil penalties and back wages against Sun Valley. Sun Valley was required to contest these penalties before an administrative law judge, with deferential review by an Article III court. Sun Valley challenged the administrative-adjudication requirement as a violation of Article III, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed with Sun Valley.

In Supreme Court briefing, the government and Sun Valley both appeal to the history-and-tradition methodology of Jarkesy, but they sharply disagree about which tradition is relevant. The government emphasizes traditions related to immigration. According to the government, its enforcement action fits within two historical categories of public rights adjudication that did not require Article III courts: rights “belonging to the sovereign, such as the right to determine whether to allow aliens into the country,” and “privileges conferred by the government, such as public benefits granted under government programs.” In the government’s view, Sun Valley violated the conditions of bringing foreign workers to the United States through an immigration program that offered the farm a benefit. The pertinent tradition is hence the history of adjudicating immigration- and benefits- related claims outside Article III courts.

Sun Valley, by contrast, casts its claim as akin to common-law breach of contract – a traditional private right requiring an Article III tribunal. DOL’s allegation, Sun Valley observes, was that Sun Valley had violated its agreement to provide certain working conditions to foreign and domestic workers. That allegation, Sun Valley contends, is simply a charge that Sun Valley breached a contract. Sun Valley further argues that DOL sought common-law remedies and in particular civil penalties – more evidence that the claim at issue involves a private right. To Sun Valley, the case is located outside the historical tradition of immigration adjudication because it is based on conditions of employment rather than immigration status. Consequently, it was unconstitutional for DOL to adjudicate Sun Valley’s dispute in-house.

Which party is right about the tradition into which the dispute over Sun Valley’s working conditions falls? Plausibly, the answer is “both.” Yes, the government is alleging that Sun Valley violated an agreement; but the agreement in question was concluded as part of an immigration program allowing Sun Valley to hire foreign workers.

So what are courts to do when, as here, they are faced with “too many traditions” – that is, traditions with different implications for the constitutional question at hand?

One possible response is to conclude that history-and-tradition analysis is hopelessly indeterminate and to reject this methodology. While many methods of constitutional interpretation fail to yield a single right answer, “history and tradition” is often justified precisely by its promise to produce constraint and fixity. Breaking this promise might be viewed as grounds for abandoning the history-and-tradition approach.

Complete repudiation of history and tradition, however, would be unwarranted. Historical practice has played an important role in both upholding and limiting non-Article III adjudication; it is a tool in judges’ toolbox and should not be thrown away.

Another option is to supplement history-and-tradition methodology, when it does not produce a clear result, with other modes of constitutional analysis. Earlier cases on non-Article III adjudication, for instance, appealed openly to practical considerations of government efficiency.

A third option would be to draw on other “modalities” of constitutional interpretation to inform the choice of which strand of tradition to emphasize. One such modality is precedent. Jarkesy did not directly confront a program like the DOL’s in Sun Valley, so it is not controlling precedent. But Jarkesy did seem to treat Congress’ broad power over immigration as a reason to uphold agency adjudication in immigration-related cases. Perhaps this suggests that DOL’s enforcement action fits better into a traditional public-rights than private-rights category.

The court may also decide to avoid the problem of too many traditions by taking a statutory “out.” When it took the case, the court added a question regarding DOL’s statutory authority to impose civil penalties and back wages on Sun Valley. The court may decide that DOL lacks such statutory authority, potentially by appealing to constitutional avoidance (in other words, construing the statute to grant DOL such authority would raise serious questions about the constitutionality of agency adjudication, which should be avoided unless necessary to decide). But the statutory question is not straightforward, and resolving it may well have ramifications for a wide array of agency-imposed penalties. At any rate, one or more of the justices can be expected to opine on Article III in Sun Valley, and the Article III issue is bound to recur.

Overall, the problem of “too many traditions” is by no means unique to the context of non-Article III adjudication. The Supreme Court faces challenging questions about how to apply history-and-tradition methodology when a present-day practice could plausibly fit into multiple traditions. The court’s response to these questions may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.

Rachel Bayefsky is Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, where she writes about civil procedure, constitutional law, and legal theory. She clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the 2018-2019 Term.

#7668. Justice Thomas will teach seminar on race, equality at University of Texas at Austin

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas answers questions during a visit to the University of Texas at Austin on April 15, 2026. (Photo by Eric Gay/The Associated Press)

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas will lead an undergraduate seminar at the University of Texas at Austin on race, equality and political thought in February.

The one-credit-hour seminar, “CIV 166 Equality and the New Birth of Freedom,” will include two hours of lecture daily from Feb. 1 to Feb. 5, 2027, for 17 students. Sixty-five applied.

Students will also meet with Justin Dyer, the dean of the University of Texas at Austin’s School of Civic Leadership, during the seminar, which follows American political thought from the nation’s founding through the Civil War to the present.

Readings include the writings and speeches of Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois, as well as civil rights leaders the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The course examines how questions of race and equality show up in recent Supreme Court decisions.

Thomas previously spoke to students and legal professionals at the University of Texas at Austin in April, making the case that the Supreme Court’s failures have stemmed from a lack of courage, not a lack of understanding, and he discussed Plessy v. Ferguson, a 1896 ruling that upheld government-enforced segregation.

Thomas, who joined the Supreme Court in 1991, is its longest-serving current member.
