#7546. The IAB has had enough: It’s calling on platforms to standardize the definition of a “view”

When YouTube changed the way it counts public views this past August, it said its main goal was helping creators get more brand deals, and get paid more for those brand deals.

The new counts, it said, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”

But the “clearer picture” that emerged was one of inaccurate inflation. Data from Agentio showed public viewcounts over-reported actual views by 40%; experiments by individual creators like John Green, who compared his backend viewcount of one video to its public-facing count, found similar inaccuracy.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, the Interactive Advertising Bureau has released a report, The Creator Economy’s Next Chapter, that calls for wide standardization of what counts as a “view.”

Accurate measurement is the “fault line beneath the creator economy,” the IAB said in its report. This overall conclusion came from 53 participating industry leaders who filled out the IAB’s survey, and also from senior industry leader interviews conducted by the IAB’s Creator Economy Board.

“Measurement also sits inside problems that look like something else. Two sides who disagree on creator pricing both agree they cannot judge whether creators are paid fairly because nobody agrees what creator content is worth,” the IAB wrote. “One in eight respondents traced budget fights with leadership to measurement gaps, and a similar share said organizations withhold results because the numbers behind them are not solid enough to publish.”

We see why this is a major concern: Brands pay creators based on their reach, so when platforms like YouTube roll out changes that inflate views, marketers end up overpaying.

It might not sound bad for creators to make a little extra cash, but this situation doesn’t end well for them either. If they secure a brand deal based on inflated views, that sets a high bar for engagement that their sponsored content almost certainly will not clear. This performance gap might result in them losing their relationship with that individual brand, or with an entire agency that represents other important brands in their niche.

It’s not just marketers that told the IAB standardization is needed. “Measurement providers, who see the problem most closely, were unanimous in choosing a common definition of a view as a top priority,” the bureau said in its report.

They also have a proposed solution: “Respondents are clear about where to start. Given 11 possible standards, two-thirds (66%) chose a common definition of a view and exposure metrics across platforms,” per the report. “Each platform counts a view differently, and shared reporting format, cross-channel planning, and any comparison with video or television all depend on counting it the same way.”

Among the IAB’s respondents, another interesting data point emerged. The majority of entities that produce metrics (like platforms, marketing agencies, and measurement companies) say they are “very confident” in the accuracy of the numbers they provide.

Meanwhile brands and talent agencies both said they have zero percent confidence in numbers they receive.

The IAB says to rectify this problem, it plans to work alongside the Media Ratings Council and other “engaged industry bodies” to bring content platforms and measurement providers together so everyone can agree on cross-platform definitions of a view, an impression, reach, and watch time.

It says it hopes to secure one to two platform agreements within the first year of this effort.

If it does that, we might be looking at one of the biggest industry shifts to date, and could end up in a radically different era of social media and content creation.

35% of respondents said creators’ work split across teams and tools is not working. 33% said brands don’t understand creators’ channels. 31% cited pricing inconsistency, and 25% said agreeing on contract and deal terms is difficult.

Solutions they suggested include standard T&Cs and contracts for creator x bran deals (66% of respondents), transparency standards for agency fee disclosure (38%), and a unified creator taxonomy (31%).

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to 10+ countries in English and launching multiturn ads in the U.S. Here is what PPC advertisers need to know about reporting.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to more than 10 new countries in English while launching multiturn ads for follow-up queries in the U.S.

Google shared the update from its official Google Ads X account on November 9, following an earlier LinkedIn post from Dan Taylor noting plans to bring ads in AI Mode to additional countries in Q4.

Eligible campaigns can already participate, though advertisers still can’t see AI Mode performance separately in Google Ads.

Here’s what’s changing, how conversational placements work, and what you need to know when clients ask about AI Mode reporting.

Google’s October announcement named 10 additional countries where ads in AI Mode are expanding:

The expansion currently supports English. Google also announced plans to bring ads in AI Mode to Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom in Q4 2026. Those markets were listed as upcoming rather than part of the initial rollout.

Google’s availability documentation notes that Pakistan supports text ads only.

Multiturn ads are launching in the U.S., allowing ads to appear on follow-up questions within an AI Mode conversation. Google hasn’t announced when those placements will expand outside the U.S.

Google describes AI Mode as a search experience for questions involving exploration, reasoning, or complex comparisons. Users can ask a detailed question an dcontinue with follow-ups as they work through their options.

AI Mode may use “query fan-out,” issuing related searches across subtopics and data sources to develop a response.

With multiturn ads, Google can show an ad during those follow-up exchanges when the conversation has commercial relevance.

According to Google’s advertiser documentation, ads can match directly to a search query or draw on context from both the question and AI response. An exploratory question can then create an advertising opportunity even when the user hasn’t searched for a specific product.

In his LinkedIn update, Taylor noted that people are asking longer, more detailed, and exploratory questions in AI Mode, and described many of those interactions as upper-funnel queries that carry commercial intent.

For advertisers, that means ads may reach people still comparing approaches or deciding what they need. A longer question or another follow-up does not, on its own, indicate that someone is ready to buy.

As ads in AI Mode expand, clients will likely ask whether their campaigns are appearing there and how those ads perform.

In my view, the most important thing for agency and in-house teams to communicate right now is that reporting is limited, and you can’t separate out AI Mode performance granularly.

Google’s reporting documentation confirms that AI Mode impressions, clicks, conversions, and costs are included in standard campaign reporting. Search terms are also combined with other traffic, without a separate AI Mode breakdown. That prevents advertisers from calculating an AI Mode-specific CPA or ROAS.

Google’s keyword prioritization documentation also says reported search terms for experiences including AI Mode may approximate the user’s intent. Advertisers should not assume they are seeing the exact question someone entered.

Teams can still review those terms for relevance, compare conversion performance, and check lead quality. If results change after the rollout, though, the timing alone can’t directly establish that AI Mode caused it.

When clients ask how AI Mode ads are performing, advertisers can explain that those results are included in campaign totals. Google Ads doesn’t report them separately, so teams can’t show how much spend or how many conversions came from AI Mode.

Google is adding countries and follow-up placements without giving advertisers a separate view of their results.

That leaves teams answering questions about AI Mode with campaign-level data. A campaign could improve overall while AI Mode underperforms, or the reverse, and the combined totals wouldn’t show that granularity.

Separate reporting would help advertisers understand which searches and placements are producing sales or qualified leads. Until Google provides it, teams can explain how their campaigns qualify for AI Mode, but can’t necessarily tell clients what those placements contributed to.

Hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual update related to the ByteDance-owned platform. During the first half of 2026, gaming streams on TikTok Live pulled in 2.5 billion hours of watch time. That traffic gave TikTok Live a 14% share of the game streaming market, pulling it even with the Stake.com-affiliated platform Kick.

Previous Hatchet reports have characterized Twitch and YouTube Gaming‘s dominant positions within the streaming landscape, but the firm’s latest dispatches have shown that TikTok Live is gaining on its market-leading rivals. While TikTok Live watch time grew 96% year-over-year, Twitch and YouTube Gaming’s respective market shares both went down.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Through properties like Hatchet, FaZe Clan, and TubeBuddy, GameSquare has made deep inroads in digital gaming communities. “Hatchet’s latest report shows just how quickly TikTok Live has established itself in gaming live-streaming,” said GameSquare CEO Justin Kenna in a statement. “Nearly doubling its gaming hours watched in a year is a clear signal that audience habits are shifting toward mobile, discovery-driven viewing.”

Kenna cited titles like Roblox, Garena Free Fire, and Mobile Legends as three major drivers of TikTok Live’s watch time uptick. Roblox led all games in terms of TikTok Live watch time during the first half of 2026; it generated 631 million hours of TikTok viewership during that period.

Roblox is a favorite of Gen Alpha gamers, while Free Fire and Mobile Legends appeal to gamers on mobile devices, especially outside of the United States. Those two data points help explain how TikTok Live has managed such a sizable gaming glow-up — it has volume none of its competitors can match. With 1.4 million creators active each day, TikTok Live’s community is nearly twice as big as Twitch’s.

That massive quantity has made TikTok Live a market leader across multiple streaming categories. Its gaming operation, however, is one of its strongest fortes, and rival platforms should be prepared to see more growth from their ByteDance-owned competitor.

#7539. The $4 million Internet Invitational might become golf’s next big thing — or another bogey

You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all. I’m talking about the Internet Invitational, which recently wrapped up its second season by splitting a $4 million prize among the 16 members of the winning team.

The driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports. To create an event that could demonstrate the influence and appeal of the “YouTube golf” scene, Portnoy teamed up with Robby Berger and his Bob Does Sports brand.

The first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize. The event was put on as a response to the PGA’s uneven investment in golf personalities. The Creator Classic that had signaled the PGA’s interest in digital partnerships was not held at TPC Sawgrass in 2026.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Portnoy and Berger bet that they could outdo the PGA by fully embracing golf creators, and they doubled down in 2026, when they quadrupled the size of the Internet Invitational prize. “It’s all because of Dave, man,” Barstool Sports video editor Brendan Jones told Golf magazine. “Dave puts up all this money, and that changes people. That’s not good or bad — it just changes the way that people act, right? Dave’s big thing with anything that we do at Barstool, it’s like, what are the stakes? Why do people care? How are we going to get anything out of them?”

In this case, people care because the proceedings were sillier, wackier, and more relatable than anything a PGA-sanctioned event could deliver. There were breakout stars like Paige Spiranac, wildly varied handicaps, and plenty of substance use during the tournament. And the fans loved it. Viewership hit 3.5 million during the first 24 hours and ballooned past 11 million views within a week.

“When you put the average Joe, who’s not a great golfer— that, to I think a lot of people, was riveting,” Berger told The Hollywood Reporter. “I mean, it’s kind of what Bob Does Sports was built off of.”

As exciting as the action may have been, the Internet Invitational wasn’t free from drama. Nelk member Salim Sirur‘s excessive drinking and Sam Heung Min‘s criticisms related to rules enforcement added controversy to the event’s conclusion. Given Portnoy’s controversial past and the indiscretions of some big names in the YouTube golf community (looking at you, Good Good), one wonders how long the Internet Invitational can sustain its positive momentum.

But the success of the tournament’s second iteration can’t be ignored. With the decline of LIV Golf and the presence of elite golfers on YouTube, there’s an opportunity for creators to build a viable alternative to the PGA Tour. To do that will take continued dedication from the people who made the Internet Invitational happen — and the golfers might want to cut down on the drinking, too.

#7537. Google’s November 2026 Core Update Starts Rolling Out via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Spend less time on publishing and reports, and more on helpful content. November 18, 2 PM ET.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Google's latest core update is rolling out worldwide in all languages. The company calls it a regular update, and rankings may move during the rollout.

Google began rolling out the November 2026 core update today, according to the Google Search Status Dashboard. The rollout started at 10:06 a.m. PT. Google says the update applies globally and to all languages and may take up to two weeks to complete.

The company’s Search Central account also announced the update on LinkedIn. It’s the third Search core update this year. Google recommends waiting until the rollout is complete before checking your Search Console data.

Google’s Search Status Dashboard entry reads:

“Released the November 2026 core update, which applies globally and to all languages. The rollout may take up to 2 weeks to complete.”

“This is a regular update designed to better surface relevant, satisfying content for searchers from all types of sites.”

The exact wording in that sentence is what Google used for its March core update.

As of posting time, no specific objectives are mentioned on either the dashboard entry or the LinkedIn post. The Search Central blog doesn’t have a post regarding the update either. Google’s core updates page carries a revision date of Dec. 10, 2025.

The May core update finished rolling out on June 2, more than five months before today’s launch. Three spam updates ran in between.

The November update is the eighth ranking update listed on the Search Status Dashboard so far this year.

Some sites may experience rank changes during the rollout of the November core update. Google’s core updates document advises waiting at least a full week after the completion of a core update, then comparing your Search Console data from that week to a week prior to the start of the rollout. Google’s suggested baseline in advance of the November update is a week prior to Nov. 10.

A full two-week rollout would finish around Nov. 24. The week immediately following Nov. 24 will include U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sites looking at this time period compared to a pre-update week would be looking at holiday traffic against a regular week.

According to Google, core updates don’t target specific sites or individual pages and are meant to keep its systems current as content on the web changes.

Per its LinkedIn post, Google will update its ranking release history page once the rollout is complete. We’ll update this article then, too.

#7535. Have you heard? MatPat’s return, Tubi CEO’s next move, and Trisha Paytas’ payday.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, a beloved couple has a new channel on YouTube, a vaunted exec has a new gig, and a much-memed creator is making bank (and hitting bookshelves).

Welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick. The man known as MatPat and his wife Stephanie haven’t shared many videos since they sold their Theorist brand nearly four years ago. But these crazy kids couldn’t stay offline forever, so they’re back with PatChat, a new channel featuring the couple’s conversations about internet culture. PatChat won’t upload nearly as frequently as the Theorist channels, and that’s ok. Let the Patricks live a little bit!

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

CNN panelist pushes back against Hasan Piker lawsuit. Piker argued that Scott Jennings defamed him by misconstruing statements that were clearly said in jest. In response, Jennings’ lawyers argued that Piker did make those statements, sarcastic or not — so they are looking to have the $72.5 million lawsuit thrown out. If commentators can be held liable for sarcasm, the internet might be in real trouble.

WhatCultureGaming launches new YouTube channel to pursue different types of content. After building a popular gaming hub, the WhatCulture team is trying something a little different with MegaWhat. The plan is to release original, personality-driven content that will give the WC team more creative freedom while still allowing them to feed the YouTube algorithm on their main channel.

Anjali Sud leaves Tubi to take point at SiriusXM. As CEO of Tubi, Sud led the transformation of the Fox-owned service, which is now a major creator hub. (She was also CEO of Vimeo before that.) Now, Sud is becoming CEO of SiriusXM, giving her a chance to work her magic in the realm of digital radio. Mike Bidgoli will take over for Sud as the new top exec at Tubi HQ.

Elevate Communications brings in TikTok vet to expand creator operations. Elevate is elevating Sam Valentine, who previously connected TikTok with luxury fashion brands as the app’s Head of Digital, Social, and Creator Services. He’ll spearhead digital and social partnerships at Elevate, where he will work with clients that are eager to build creator programs in sectors like sports, entertainment, and healthcare.

Meta brings in well-traveled exec to be the VP of its in-house content studio. After a long stint at NBC News, as well as stops at Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, Rich Latour has arrived at Meta. He will be put in charge of a studio that emphasizes Meta’s brand and highlights its impact across various communities and industries.

Trisha Paytas has a book out (and she makes $100,000 a week on YouTube). While promoting her memoir Crying on the Kitchen Floor, which was recently published by Hachette, Paytas told Andy Cohen that her YouTube earnings can hit six figures during a good week. Oh, and she also has a new dating show that is rolling out on Tubi. Slow down, Trish!

Hulu taps Tinx to revive The Circle (now with TikTok voting). The creator born Christina Najjar is taking the hosting role in a new version of the reality competition series that previously aired on Netflix. Tinx will have big shoes to fill replacing previous host Michelle Buteau, but with help from the voting audience, she can ensure that the Circle revival doesn’t miss a beat.

The first Clio Creator Awards will fete Dhar Mann. Actor Terry Crews will host as the notable advertising award ceremony expands to the realm of creator content. Dhar Mann, YouTube moralist and engineer of many a brand partnership, will receive an inaugural honorary award at the new ceremony.

Kind works with a Savannah Banana to sell a TikTok-exclusive foodstuff. Baseball player Jackson Olson has amassed a significant TikTok following after getting a roster spot on the best-known “Banana Ball” team. Olson is now parlaying his influence to sell a new type of Kind bar that celebrates World Kindness Day — and is only available for purchase via TikTok Shop.

GTA VI codes are flying around on Kick and Twitch ahead of launch day. All of the major platforms want creators to play GTA VI on their services once the game launches, and giving out free copies is a good way to engender that loyalty. At this point, I’m wondering if GTA VI will be able to live up to its immersurable hype, or if viewers will tire of it after it because the main topic of conversation everywhere.

Barbie and Hot Wheels are on TikTok Shop this holiday season. TikTok continues to onboard name brands as it prepares for its most lucrative holiday season shopping spree. So if someone on your list has their eyes on some Mattel products, deals on those items will be hitting TikTok Shop in no time.

Celebs are consenting to having their voices cloned for AI ads. Ogilvy and CAA have teamed up for a partnership that will make a-list talent more accessible for advertisers and agencies that rely on generative AI pipelines. George Clooney is a CAA client, but if he goes along with this, I’m going to have no choice but to start calling him George Cloney.

Shaq is good at dunking, but can he hide in plain sight? The Big Diesel has a new gig: An ABC series that will ask contestants to hide the 7’1″ goliath in plain sight. I think, to be fair, the contestants should get to start by hiding Kevin Hart before working their way up to Shaq.

Another impulse spending deterrent is taking off in China. The WeChat mini-app dubbed ‘Wallet, Please Wait’ lets users decide whether strangers will be able to hold off on big purchases. I would be more interested in app that lets me vote on whether a stranger should be able to tell a stranger how to spend their money.

Meta removed ‘train’ from its crawl clause, kept ‘develop’, then paused everything. The pushback worked once. Do not expect it to work twice.

Meta backed down this time. On Nov. 5, it paused new business terms that would have let it crawl the website of every business using Facebook or Instagram, after publishers, a court, and a regulator pushed back. Pushback can work. But a business that gets its customers through Meta should plan as if Meta will never get better for it.

In October 2026, Meta previewed new business terms, the rules a business accepts when it uses Facebook or Instagram for business: a Page, ads, a shop. The first version let Meta use automated software to read the websites tied to a business, to “provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain” its products. Accepting was the price of staying, and the only way to say no was to stop using Meta for business.

On Oct. 16, Meta took the word “train” out and limited the crawl to its advertising and business products. “Develop” stayed in, and so did the crawl. On Oct. 23, Meta moved the start date from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20.

Meta doesn’t say why it paused. Paused is not withdrawn. Nieman Lab reports Meta’s notice says “our existing terms remain in effect”, and nothing in it says what comes back, or when.

Meta has done things that work for Meta since forever, with no regard for anyone. This is what Meta does. Hollywood has made two films about Facebook, and neither is about how well it treats its users.

Meta’s pattern feels like a slow death for a business in the Meta ecosystem, with nothing it can do about what Meta changes. Reaching for a business’s website is new. The attitude isn’t new: Meta not caring about its business users, and trying to give them no options.

So start investing in other acquisition channels, or at least planning for them.

Meta backed down this time. Do not wait for it to do it again.

This post was originally published on No Hacks.

Featured Image: Jack_the_sparow/Shutterstock

No. On Nov. 5, 2026, Meta paused them. Its Business Help Center says the updates to its Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms will not take effect on Nov. 20, 2026, and Nieman Lab reports the notice says the existing terms remain in effect. Meta has not said what comes back, or when.

Under the terms Meta previewed in October 2026, a business using Facebook or Instagram for business would have agreed to let Meta’s automated software read its website for Meta’s ads and business products, with no opt-out short of leaving. Those terms are paused. A Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab that robots.txt preferences are respected.

Yes. On Oct. 30, 2026 the U.K.’s Competition and Markets Authority opened a formal investigation into whether Meta’s commercial terms for businesses using its platforms breach competition law, under the Competition Act 1998. The CMA set no deadline and has made no decision.

Curb unwanted Google Ads spending without losing valuable conversions by weighing bidding targets, Performance Max channel grouping, and allocation limits.

Google Ads’ new Channel Prioritization and Budget Allocation controls give PPC managers more input into decisions they’ve been leaving to automation. Advertisers can choose which eligible channels receive budget first and limit spending on lower-priority inventory.

The announcement gives advertisers more options, but choosing a setting still requires a reason to intervene. A campaign meeting its CPA or ROAS target may be spending in ways the business wants to change. Restricting that spending could address the concern, although it could also reduce conversions the advertiser would want to keep.

Before applying the new controls, PPC managers need to know what each setting can change and how they’ll judge the result. A shift in channel spending alone won’t establish that the account is performing better, especially if total conversion volume falls with it.

This article examines where advertisers gain control and how to decide whether an account needs an adjustment. Performance Max is worth digging into first because the channel breakdown advertisers can see in reporting goes further than the individual priorities these settings let them assign.

Google groups Search, YouTube, Discover, Gmail, and Maps together as “Google channels” under the new prioritization settings. Advertisers can prioritize that group separately from Search Partners and the Google Display Network, but they can’t assign different priorities within it.

If you’re a PPC manager reviewing Performance Max channel results, this limits the changes you can make directly. Seeing stronger returns from Search than YouTube doesn’t create an option to give Search priority access to the campaign budget.

The controls can address a concern about partner spending. Limiting Search Partners, however, still leaves Google deciding how to distribute spending across its owned channels. Advertisers shouldn’t expect the money withheld from partners to move specifically into Search.

If your business needs separate Search and YouTube budgets, that requirement still needs to inform campaign structure. Whether restructuring is worth the additional management depends on how firmly those budgets need to be separated.

Even where advertisers can assign separate priorities, the campaign-level bidding targets still apply. A campaign using Target CPA or Target ROAS won’t be allowed to buy more expensive inventory simply because the advertiser marked it high priority.

See also: Why Do Budgets Overspend Even With A Target ROAS or CPA? – Ask A PPC

A priority setting can affect allocation when channels compete for a limited campaign budget. With Target CPA or Target ROAS bidding, Google also considers whether additional spending can meet the target.

Say you’ve got a Search campaign that regularly exhausts its budget, and Google Search produces more qualified leads than Search Partners. Giving Google Search high priority lets you favor it when allocating that limited budget.

Google still evaluates the available traffic against the bidding target. If additional Search spending would exceed it, lower-priority inventory can receive budget when Google expects that inventory to meet the target.

That leaves you, the PPC manager, with a decision about how strongly you prefer Search. Your brand may be comfortable paying more for its leads, but changing the priority doesn’t communicate a willingness to accept a higher CPA. The bidding target would need a separate review at the campaign level.

Maximize Conversions and Maximize Conversion Value campaigns without a target work differently. Google funds high-priority inventory first, then makes remaining budget available to lower-priority channels when it cannot fully spend on the preferred inventory.

For Target CPA or Target ROAS campaigns without budget constraints, Google says priority tiers generally won’t change allocation. Allocation limits still apply.

Consider a campaign consistently spending $600 against a $1,000 average daily budget, without exhausting its budget on individual days. Lowering Search Partners’ priority may change little because both networks already have budget available.

If you’re wanting to limit partner spending in that campaign, you would first need to consider an allocation percentage. Before choosing one, check the dollar amount it represents: The percentage uses the configured budget, not actual spending.

Google calculates the allocation percentage using the campaign’s average daily budget. If the campaign spends less than that budget, a lower-priority channel can receive a larger share of actual spending than the percentage suggests.

In this example below, it keeps the budget and allocation settings unchanged:

In the second row, the channel receives 25% of actual spending without exceeding the $100 represented by the setting. The advertiser has set a spending allowance that won’t necessarily maintain a 90/ten split.

Google also applies allocation limits above 0% on a best-effort basis, so daily spending can exceed the intended amount. Google says a 0% allocation prevents spending on the channel.

Before saving a percentage, calculate what it allows in dollars and check that amount against the spending you intended. Revisit it when changing the campaign budget, too. Increasing the budget from $1,000 to $2,000 doubles the allowance under an unchanged 10% setting.

An increase intended to capture more Search demand could expand partner spending as well. When raising the campaign budget, check whether the existing allocation percentage still reflects what you’re willing to spend on that network.

The controls may be available in your account before you have a clear direction on how to use them. Start with the campaigns where network spending has raised a concern, and review the results before deciding what to change.

The checks below can help you choose where to apply a restriction and assess whether it improves performance.

See also: Google Ads Bid Strategy Testing: What Changed In 2026

Start by looking at what happens after someone converts. A network taking more budget than you expected may still be bringing in qualified leads or profitable sales.

In Search campaigns, use Network (with search partners) to compare results across networks. For Performance Max, go to Campaigns → Insights and reports → Channel performance and select the campaign.

If the campaign tracks several conversion actions, review them separately. Give leads enough time to qualify before judging their quality. The same CPA can look very different once the sales team follows up, as this made-up example shows:

Both networks bring in form submissions at $100 each, but qualified leads from Search Partners cost four times as much. Limiting that spending could help while the team investigates why fewer leads qualify. Sharing qualified lead or sales data with Google could also help bidding account for the difference.

For ecommerce, check how returns and product costs affect the sales each network brings in. A higher acquisition cost may be worth paying if those customers are more profitable in the long run.

Start with a campaign where you’ve identified a reason to change network-level spending. Applying the same settings across the account could affect campaigns that are already performing well.

Before making the change, note the campaign’s budget and bidding target so you can track what changed. Decide what you need to see afterward. Using the lead example above, that might mean spending less on unqualified inquiries without losing qualified leads.

In Search, open Campaign settings → Channel Prioritization to set campaign-specific priorities and an optional allocation percentage. Check which controls are available for the campaign type you’re working on.

Avoid changing bidding targets or targeting at the same time, where possible. Otherwise, it will be harder to tell what the channel setting accomplished.

If the campaign uses a shared budget, check the other campaigns using it before saving. The allocation applies across that shared budget, so the change can affect more than the campaign you opened.

Account-level defaults can save time once you know the same approach makes sense for other campaigns. Until then, a campaign-level change gives you a smaller starting point to review.

Search campaigns with Display enabled need a settings review before Google retires the existing Display Expansion allocation setup in February 2027.

To keep the current configuration, Google recommends setting Display to Low priority with a 50% daily budget allocation. That percentage reflects the existing setup; it isn’t Google’s recommended allowance for a new Display test.

Find the Search campaigns with Display enabled and check how much they currently spend on that network. If you want to maintain the setup, use Google’s recommended migration settings and monitor spending after the change.

You can choose a lower allocation if the results justify it. Note that you’re intentionally reducing Display’s allowance, so anyone reviewing performance knows the campaign settings changed beyond the migration itself.

Once the settings have had time to affect ad delivery, the channel spending report can help show what changed. A larger Search share might look encouraging, but it could simply mean partner spending fell while Search spending stayed flat.

That could still be a good result. In the lead generation example, spending less on unqualified leads would help if qualified lead volume held steady. For ecommerce, a drop in spend would be less appealing if profitable sales disappeared along with it.

Those results may take longer to show up than the spending change itself. Leads still need follow-up, and recent clicks may turn into purchases later. The first few days of reporting may say more about the new spending mix than its effect on the business.

Google says the controls can be used in custom experiments, but experiments with multi-campaign shared budgets aren’t supported, and in those cases all channels are treated as the same priority tier. If your campaign runs on a shared budget, a before/after comparison may be your only option.

A before/after comparison can still help, although a promotion or seasonal change could explain some of the difference. The channel settings won’t necessarily deserve all the credit, or blame.

The limit may be worth keeping if it cuts wasted spend without hurting sales. If it saves money but costs the business profitable customers, loosening it could be the better choice.

See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It

PPC managers already decide how much they’re willing to spend on different networks. Until now, acting on those decisions has sometimes meant excluding inventory or changing campaign structure. These settings give advertisers another option when they want to limit spending without shutting a network off entirely.

That could make it easier to revisit an earlier exclusion or address a spending concern within an existing campaign. Google still decides how to allocate much of the budget, particularly across its owned channels in Performance Max. The additional control gives advertisers more room to manage that spending, even if it doesn’t reach every decision they’d like to make.

#7529. In the AI age, publishers who understand what readers want will do best, a new report argues

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

AI inverts the traditional journalism hierarchy: Instead of reporters gathering information, editors deciding how to present it, and newsrooms releasing the same final story to everyone, AI agents deliver what readers ask for, refining or expanding on information as requested.

It’s “an interactive process in a way the current news system isn’t,” write the authors of “The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an AI-Intermediated Age,” released Wednesday by the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY. (The cake’s three layers are “the products that identify what people want to know, the systems that synthesize answers, and the organizations that produce the underlying reporting.”)

Some interesting ideas from the report by Gina Chua and Adiel Kaplan:

This new age may be better for some readers. The authors write:

There are people the old system never reached, or never reached well. A parent who hears of school budget cuts may want to know if their child’s elementary school art class will survive. No newsroom would assign that story. It matters to a handful of families whose children attend a single school, and the exact answer is uncertain. A well-designed AI system could pull together what is known from reporting and context and offer a nuanced response — fulfilling an information need that previously did not have enough economic power to be met directly.

Similarly, minority communities whose concerns didn’t rise to the level of interest of a city newspaper might have rarely seen their perspectives reflected in coverage in the past. Coverage in the mainstream media of the AIDS epidemic in the early 1980s was often focused on the risk to the heterosexual population rather than on the gay community it ravaged. An AI system that can access information from and about underserved communities could rectify that.

Publishers opting out could make the information environment worse. If news organizations seek to prevent AI from using their content, they may contribute to a poorer “information commons,” the authors argue. It “works as a strategy for individual organizations, but cedes the broader mission of providing information to the vast majority of the public to others who may not have the public’s interests at heart.”

Scoops and exclusives are a “luxury” — and they’re losing value fast.

Even a pivot to investigative reporting, as important a public good as that is, is not necessarily a solution. Much of investigative journalism is summarizable once it is published, even if the original story breaks important news and is a delight to read. As Francesco Marconi noted, a multi-month investigation could cost a newsroom $200,000 in resources, then drop in economic value to close to zero within minutes of publication. Both investigations and scoops can have huge social value and help build a brand, but economically, they provide little lasting value to their newsrooms — and even less so in an AI-intermediated landscape. “Commoditized news” isn’t saving anyone. Publishers have to make “hard choices” about what they’ll cover, the authors write: In an AI-intermediated world, commoditized news carries little value, especially if it’s already available in some other form. That’s not to say that day-to-day coverage of municipal government, a core task of many local newsrooms, should go away; only that its coverage needs to be differentiated from what could be found elsewhere or summarized from a meeting transcript, for it to hold value. Differentiation might involve adding context to the coverage through original reporting, or asking questions that wouldn’t otherwise be asked at a press conference. The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

#7526. The Ringer bets on Substack’s network over its own website

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Once synonymous with independent writers, Substack is increasingly home to established publishers.

“Very interesting that The Ringer’s writers write on Substack and not…The Ringer.” “What’s the point of the website then?” “Hold up. You’re telling me The Ringer would rather make money on writing than not make money on writing?”

These were some of the responses after The Ringer’s Zach Lowe announced his new newsletter. The Lowe Post, which covers the NBA, joins The Ringer’s Sean Fennessey, Tom Pelissero, and Bryan Curtis on Substack. (The Lowe Post is $10 a month, and has already become one of Substack’s bestselling sports newsletters. Fennessey’s newsletter is $5 a month; Pelissero’s is $8 a month, and Curtis’s is free.)

Though podcasting has been his main gig for a while now, Zach Lowe is one of the best sports writers in the country — witty, warm-hearted, and a true lover of basketball and the Mets. In his inaugural newsletter, he wrote about how he feels his sports analysis loses a step when he’s only talking, not writing.

On the one hand, of course Lowe should have a newsletter. But his Substack, and those of his colleagues, are not independent side hustles. Each has Spotify and The Ringer branding.

As a digital media business, The Ringer has always been flexible and opportunistic. It was initially published on Medium when it launched in 2016. The publication moved to an ad and tech partnership with Vox in 2017. It was acquired by Spotify for $250 million in 2020 and, five years later, signed a distribution deal with Netflix to bring some of its video podcasts (including The Bill Simmons Show, The Zach Lowe Show, and The Rewatchables) to the platform. The website has always been free to read.

The Ringer declined to comment on its Substack strategy and would not tell me whether the writers receive a share of subscription revenue. (The lack of comment has garnered its own press coverage.) Though The Ringer has referred to the new newsletters as being in “partnership” with Substack, there’s no separate financial relationship between the two companies, Substack confirmed.

If you find this a little strange, you’re not wrong. The Substack-Ringer whatever-this-is is a confusing move that is raising a lot of very 2026 questions. Here are some things I’m wondering.

While Grantland — the beloved sports writing site created by Ringer founder Bill Simmons in 2011 and shuttered by ESPN in 2015 — was known for its long-form journalism, The Ringer is all-in on podcasts. Simmons jokes on nearly every episode of his own show that his “fingers stopped working” years ago and that his days writing columns are behind him.

Today, most of the links on The Ringer’s homepage will bring you somewhere else. The homepage’s function is closer to a landing page or linktree than a news website. Many links redirect to Spotify, where listeners can watch or listen to Ringer podcasts. Now, with the newsletter launches, several links whisk you off The Ringer and over to Substack.

Burned by Facebook and forever-shifting algorithmic winds, many publishers have focused on building on their own channels in recent years. The theory is that direct-to-reader news products like newsletters, apps, and events will help publishers control audience connections and insulate them from inevitable platform pivots.

But though Substack was once synonymous with independent writers, its perks are luring more and more established publications onto the platform. Some, like The Ringer, are sharing Substack-exclusive content. Others, like New York magazine and The Wall Street Journal, are redistributing work that exists elsewhere on the internet.

One major pull? Substack has morphed into a full-on social media platform, albeit one where publishers can directly monetize and capture email addresses for themselves.

In the past six months, the app has generated nearly 800,000 paid subscriptions, according to Substack, and more than half of those subscriptions came directly from its Twitter-like Notes feed. Network effects account for more than half of all subscriptions on the platform and about 30% of paid subscriptions, a spokesperson said.

Media journalist Simon Owens has been tracking the rise of traditional media outlets on Substack (on Substack, naturally).

“Open web” is an ill-defined concept. Sometimes people use it to mean the public portion of the internet that’s indexable by search engines. Others mean, basically, websites — anything you can reach on a web browser at a URL. Whatever the semantics, people have been shoveling dirt on “the open web” for years. (This New York Times obituary noting the rise of paywalls, apps, and tiers of access was published back in 2010.) But the death notices have picked up with the rise of AI.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026Google Search referrals to publisher websites are down 40.2% year over year, according to Chartbeat. And AI chatbots are not sending users to news sites. Referrals from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and the like were just 0.01% of traffic to publishers and declining, Chartbeat found.

Even before it was acquired by Spotify, The Ringer’s primary business was podcasts, so it’s never been as reliant on search as text-first publishers. The Ringer can afford to deprioritize its website more than most. But all kinds of publishers are having to respond to a real shift in the way people consume news and content.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat’s it take to make a great daily newsletter? Axios’ Kendall Baker is planning to bring one to Yahoo SportsJoshua BentonAugust 17, 2023Kendall Baker, senior writer and head of newsletters for Yahoo Sports, knows a thing or two about email newsletters. He says The Ringer’s move exemplifies a news consumption trend that’s only picking up speed.

“Most people’s general way of finding information or consuming information online is that they’re opening their phone and going straight to a social media app and starting to scroll,” Baker said.

Another app that most U.S. adults open up every day? Their email.

“If I want an engaged audience on a daily basis, relying on them coming to find me versus going to them would be silly — and it’s becoming more and more silly,” he said. “I think that’s partially what’s driving this. Newsletters are an obvious solution there.”

The Ringer’s move is also a bet on the strength of individual personalities. Substack doesn’t (yet) offer bundles, so a reader who wants all of The Ringer’s paid Substack content will have to fork over something like $23/month — more than a subscription to New York magazine or Apple News and a little less than a full New York Times bundle. Even with the strong parasocial relationships The Ringer enjoys — enough to fuel many, many subreddits — the pricing was a common complaint online.

Many publishers will not want to cannibalize pricier subscriptions by selling access to a single popular writer. Offering a whole-site subscription also lets readers discover (and hopefully fall in love with!) more of your content.

“It seems in the Substack era, you’re writing for people who really like you,” Simmons said on a recent podcast about sportswriting. “And you’re getting that audience but then, how do you pull other people in? That’s going to be the big question over the next five to 10 years.”

“Obviously we have a lot of writing on The Ringer dot com that we’re very proud of,” Simmons added, pointing to a NFL Take-O-Meter piece by The Ringer’s Austin Gayle. “But will it ever be like 2011 again? I don’t know.”

“You mean, when we launched Grantland?” The Ringer’s Bryan Curtis asked.

“No, just that era. How many writers were coming up — the energy behind it, and all the different styles,” Simmons said. “I wonder if we’ll ever have that many writers again trying that many different things.”

#7524. Publishers pressure Meta to nix new terms that would let the company scrape their websites

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30.

In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.”

The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

“News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey said in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their users), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.”

NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey said, should focus on four core issues:

(i) the specific Meta Company Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content;

(ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products;

(iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized;

(iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected.

Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.”

The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its new subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world.

The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.”

“If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” said CMDG director Courtney Radsch. “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.”

On Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.”

“The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” said Tim Cowen, a MOW cofounder.

MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter, who said during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with company representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the new terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review.

On Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s new terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.”

“Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026The Association of Information Media (AMI) in Spain, which represents more than 100 news outlets in the country, echoed its support of the letter in a statement on Thursday.

“Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.”

#7520. Meta delays rollout of terms that would allow broad scraping of news sites. Legal experts are still skeptical.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Meta’s new commercial terms will go into effect three weeks later than initially planned.

RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Meta has delayed the effective date of its new terms of service for business accounts to November 20 in the face of mounting pressure from the global news industry.

Nieman Lab first reported on the terms on October 15. They would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. Virtually every news organization has at least one business account. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.”

The terms were previously set to take effect on October 30, with no way to opt out, setting off an outcry from news publishers, politicians, and press associations on both sides of the Atlantic.

“We are extending the effective date of our updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to November 20 to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not — including how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” a Meta spokesperson told Nieman Lab in a statement Friday.

A Meta spokesperson said on October 17 that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

As of October 23, Meta has made no other changes to the terms aside from the implementation date. No versions of the terms include language about respecting robots.txt preferences.

“Publishers should always be concerned about tech companies attempting to take content for free, and should assume that Meta is taking this additional time to either find a new way to try to mislead publishers into granting Meta free access to valuable copyrighted content or finally give up in the face of pressure,” said Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “Publishers don’t need more PR statements or explanations. They need Meta to keep its hands off their copyrighted material and respect publishers’ terms of service.”

“I don’t think that repeating the same non-explanations for another three weeks will make much difference,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, added. “But maybe they’ll use the time to come up with better explanations.”

Thomas Höppner, a professor and attorney specializing in competition law in Germany, told Nieman Lab that “Meta’s conduct constitutes a prima facie infringement of European Union competition law, and a textbook case for imposing interim measures.”

The postponement could be a legal strategy that the company is exploring, he said.

“My fear is that this is merely a measure by Meta to reduce the risk of court actions for interim measures,” Höppner said. “If affected parties wait too long from the day of knowledge of the changes [until] the filing of an action, a court will assume that the matter cannot be urgent — and deny interim relief on this ground…Under some jurisdictions, a platform needs to give business users appropriate warning before implementing measures. It may well be that Meta just tries to reduce the risk of losing on the ground not having sufficiently informed business users about its new terms.”

News publishers and press associations have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect, and on Meta to include specific language about respecting publishers’ crawling preferences.

On Thursday, the News/Media Alliance in the United States sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, demanding that the company suspend the terms before October 30. The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on the same day.

Multiple European press associations signed a joint letter to the European Commission, citing potential violations of the Digital Markets Act and calling for intervention. Earlier this week, two German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review has been conducted.

In the United Kingdom, the Competition and Market Authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss the terms. In a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday, executive director Will Hayter said he had a meeting scheduled with the company on Wednesday to learn more about the terms.

“The CMA has been in urgent discussions with Meta this week on this important issue,” a CMA spokesperson said on Friday. “Meta has now paused implementation until 20 November. We will continue to scrutinize these terms and engage with Meta and others as we consider our next steps.”

Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K’s News Media Association, wrote on LinkedIn on Friday that “this delay is welcome, but it is a pause not a solution.”

#7519. I went looking for the source of one little statistic. That was easier said than done.

The claim: 75% of your emotions are generated by smell. It had to come from somewhere, right?

Apparently, 75% of your emotions are generated by smell.

Or that’s what the internet says, anyway. The statistic appears everywhere from marketing books and articles to academic papers about the power of scent. As a perfumer (someone who creates fragrances) and journalist who writes about these things, I came across it several times, and when I finally wanted to cite it for an article about the impact of scent on mood and memory, I went looking for the original research.

This wasn’t a totally new experience for me. One time, while working on a workplace story as the editor of a hospitality trade magazine, I couldn’t find the source of an employee retention statistic, so I wrote the people who included it in a study. They wrote back to say they had no idea what I was talking about.

In this case, there was no such dead end. I followed link after link, figuring surely I would get to the bottom of it, but every source pointed to another source, which pointed to another, and somehow none of them led to the original research I was looking for.

I asked ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude for help. They gave me links to wellness blogs, aromatherapy companies, and authoritative-looking PDF reports. But as I ruled each one out as the original source, the answers became more circular, and the trail ate itself.

Me: Where did the statistic that 75% of emotions are generated by smell come from?

Google Gemini The Sense of Smell Institute.

Gemini: There isn’t a specific study. The statistic was popularized through scent marketing research.

Gemini: Martin Lindstrom’s 2005 book Brand Sense.

Me: Does the book contain the original research?

Gemini: Lindstrom commissioned extensive research into sensory branding through the research firm Millward Brown.

Me: Does that research establish that 75 percent of emotions are generated by smell?

Gemini: Would you like to know how lavender and citrus can influence your mood?

Lindstrom did look like a real lead. Several writers and businesses traced the number to the Danish author’s 2005 book Brand Sense: Sensory Secrets Behind the Stuff We Buy. Simon & Schuster’s page for the book says it outright: “Research shows that a full 75% of our emotions are in fact generated by what we smell.” Aha!

I bought the book and read it. While there is talk of emotions and the senses, the number isn’t in there.

Next, I wrote to Lindstrom’s company asking them to point me toward the original research. They sent me a link to a copy of Brand Sense and told me I would find the research in the book.

I tried another route. Brand Sense was based in large part on an international study by market research company Millward Brown. The 75% figure has been attributed directly to that research. So I went looking for the Millward Brown study. But I couldn’t find it anywhere.

There were other questions: Does the stat even make scientific sense? How would you measure the percentage of emotions generated by smell? Do people with no sense of smell experience 75% fewer emotions? And what about emotions that seem to have nothing to do with the senses at all, like grief over someone’s death, a breakup, or anxiety over losing your job?

I asked Kristen Lindquist, a social and affective neuroscientist and psychology professor at Ohio State University who studies emotion. She had never heard of the statistic.

“I imagine if somebody had done that study I would be aware of it,” she told me.

There is a relationship between smell and emotion, and it may be possible to measure something like this, she said. Researchers could, for example, ask people throughout the day how they’re feeling and whether what they’re feeling is related to something they’re seeing, hearing, touching or smelling. But that still wouldn’t make emotion the product of one sense. “Emotions really arise from all of our sensations,” Lindquist said, including signals from within our bodies. Our brains process all of that information together to figure out what is happening and what it means for us.

RELATED ARTICLERepetition makes climate misinformation feel more true — even for those who back climate scienceYangxueqing Mary JiangAugust 12, 2024There’s a name for the particular way an unsupported claim can acquire the appearance of fact through citation: citogenesis. Coined by Randall Munroe in an XKCD comic, the term describes the process by which an unsupported claim gets repeatedly cited until the citations themselves make it look like truth.

I called Jodi Schneider, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison Information School whose research includes scientific evidence and citation integrity, to talk about it. I sent her the 75% statistic, and she went looking for the source herself.

“It was not a casual ‘Let me look for 20 minutes, and there it is,'” she told me. “I would find a thing, [it] would go to something else, and that would be a dead end.”

The problem, Schneider said, is that repeating a claim is much easier than investigating it. “Somebody says something, it sounds like a thing you’d like to know or repeat, and you don’t trace it back to where it came from. You just pass it on.” Then repetition becomes the “evidence,” and “if you hear the same thing from multiple places, it’s harder to question.”

This psychological phenomenon is known as the illusory truth effect: We’re more likely to believe information we’ve encountered before. The effect was first demonstrated in the 1970s and has since been replicated many times. More unsettlingly, research has found that repetition can make a false claim seem more believable even when it contradicts something we know to be true.

In other words, seeing the same statistic everywhere doesn’t just make it look well sourced; it makes it feel true.

It’s hard to fully check every claim. Writers build arguments from dozens of pieces of information, and tracing each one all the way back to its origin can take an absurd amount of time.

Newsrooms have spent years cutting staff and budgets, including the fact-checkers and copy editors whose job was to catch this kind of thing. At the same time, the volume of information journalists have to sort through has exploded. Finding a source for a claim can take seconds. Establishing where it actually came from can take hours (or an eternity).

Meanwhile, the consequences of not checking facts compound. Once a bad claim gets published, it becomes another source for the next journalist, another search result for the next reader and another apparent confirmation that the claim must be true.

AI is making that problem worse. It repeats the same unsupported claims while stripping away some of the clues that might otherwise make us suspicious of the source.

“The polish that generative AI can put on just about anything is already a challenge,” Schneider said. More importantly, “Generative AI is really, really good at being persuasive, even if the claims inside the persuasion have no basis in reality.”

Most people are not going to track a statistic through six articles, buy the book everyone cites, email the author, and start calling academics. They don’t have the time or energy for that, and they shouldn’t have to do it anyway. One of journalism’s roles is to provide information that’s more reliable than TikTok or whatever nonsense Google Gemini spits out.

When we get it wrong, we don’t just add another bad source to the pile. We give the claim credibility and put it in front of more people. And once they’ve seen it, the illusory truth effect suggests they’re more likely to believe it the next time. (Research has also found that repeated misinformation is more likely to be repeated than new misinformation, and can continue to influence people even after it has been corrected.)

Nobody is going to die because they believe smell generates 75 percent of their emotions. But replace that claim with one about a vaccine, a war, an election or a medical treatment and the same failure becomes considerably less benign.

That’s why the difference between finding a source and finding the source matters. I found hundreds of sources for the 75% statistic. I still haven’t found the source. That doesn’t mean it’s not out there.

Can you find the source of the 75% stat? Email [email protected].

Elizabeth Bromstein is a writer, editor, and perfumer.
